Formulation
- Predisposing factors: Chronic medical conditions (type 2 diabetes, hypertension) which may influence infection severity and recovery.
- Precipitating factors: Acute viral respiratory infection beginning 5–6 days ago with dry cough, rhinorrhea, chills and myalgias.
- Perpetuating factors: Ongoing nocturnal cough disrupting sleep leading to fatigue and decreased activity; continued attendance at work early in illness.
- Protective factors: Supportive partner, regular GP follow-up, adherence to chronic disease medications.
- Summary: A likely self-limiting viral respiratory illness causing persistent dry cough and systemic symptoms in a patient with controlled diabetes and hypertension; sleep disruption and fatigue are current significant sequelae. Advice given for symptomatic care and follow-up if not improving.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Acute viral respiratory illness with persistent dry cough
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Recover from infection and return to normal activities/work
  - Improve sleep and reduce nocturnal coughing
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Symptom relief (cough, myalgia, chills)
  - Monitor for complication or secondary bacterial infection; initiate further care if symptoms persist or worsen
- Actions (Patient):
  - Rest and take 1–2 days off work if able
  - Maintain adequate oral fluids and hydration
  - Use regular paracetamol for fever/aches as needed
  - Reduce alcohol intake (clinician suggested gradual reduction)
  - Return for review if no improvement in 2–3 days or sooner if breathing worsens
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Provide symptomatic management advice and safety-netting
  - Review patient if not improving in 2–3 days; consider antibiotics if persistent fever or nonresolving cough suggestive of secondary bacterial chest infection
  - Issue medical certificate/sick leave as clinically indicated

Secondary Problem: Sleep disturbance and daytime fatigue secondary to nocturnal cough
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Improve sleep quality and daytime energy
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Reduce nocturnal coughing frequency/intensity to restore sleep
- Actions (Patient):
  - Implement strategies to improve sleep (bed rest, head elevation if helpful, avoid alcohol before bed)
  - Continue hydration and symptomatic measures
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Reinforce symptomatic measures and follow-up plan; reassess sleep disturbance at follow-up visit

Tertiary Problem: Chronic medical comorbidities (Type 2 diabetes, hypertension)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Maintain control of diabetes and blood pressure during acute illness
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Ensure continued adherence to medications and monitoring during illness
- Actions (Patient):
  - Continue regular medications (Metformin and Lisinopril) as prescribed; monitor glucose as advised
  - Seek medical review if unable to maintain oral intake or if glucose/BP control deteriorates
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Continue routine management of chronic conditions; reinforce medication adherence; review if complications arise

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Nature of probable viral illness and expected duration (commonly 7–10 days)
  - Symptomatic self-care: rest, fluids, paracetamol
  - Advice to reduce alcohol intake (suggested staged reduction)
  - When to seek earlier review (worsening breathing, persistent fever, nonimproving cough)
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - Increasing breathlessness or difficulty breathing
  - Ongoing or worsening fever
  - Cough not improving after 2–3 days from consultation (or by 7–10 days as per clinician judgement)
- Coping Strategies:
  - Rest, limit physical activity while symptomatic, maintain hydration, use paracetamol for symptomatic relief, take brief time off work to recover

Consent, Coordination & Review
- Patient Consent to Plan:
  - Not explicitly recorded; patient agreed to the advice given in consultation
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient:
  - Not recorded
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care:
  - Not recorded
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional):
  - Not recorded
- Review Date:
  - Return for review if not improving in 2–3 days; sooner if breathing worsens

Quality checks
● Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Formal mental health diagnosis, suicide/self-harm risk screening, detailed mental status cognitive testing, exact medication doses, emergency contact details, documented consent to written care plan.
● Internal conflicts from the transcript:
  - Medication name conflict: clinician referred to "Lisinopril" and then "Zinopril" — recorded as conflict noted.
● Transcript quality notes:
  - Transcript largely coherent; minor overlapping/short pauses and occasional unclear single words but overall content adequate for documentation.
